minutes.headline: Task force heard advisers explain prudent-investor law for trust funds, then reviewed town and school spending comparisons; no votes.
minutes.summary: Two investment advisers explained the new prudent-investor law and which of the town's money buckets it covers; the task force asked about raising yield on general-fund cash. Members then presented DLS spending comparisons for the town and school side, discussing debt service, health insurance, recycling costs, busing, special education and teacher pay. The only motion was to adjourn; follow-ups were assigned on investments, an accounting question and stakeholder input.

budget_items.topic: Per capita general fund expenditure and category comparisons from DLS
budget_items.what_was_said: Per capita spending rose FY19 to FY23; education is about half the budget; Lunenburg compared to 29 other towns.
Health insurance spending rose sharply after a pandemic dip, with Lunenburg's FY23 percent increase second highest among comparison towns.
Debt service is a little over a tenth of expenditures in FY23; officials said paid-off debt has been absorbed elsewhere so there is no source to cover new non-excluded debt.
Debt service is expected to fall between FY25 and FY28 as excludable debt is paid off.

The town pays per ton for recycling, with net cost depending on market value of materials; options to be presented to the select board.
Anticipated per-student out-of-district tuition and number of placements were stated; a behavior analyst position was credited with stabilizing placements.

budget_items.topic: Circuit breaker reimbursement and cost shock
budget_items.what_was_said: A member said late-arriving students create cost shocks because reimbursement trails, and that behavior analyst positions can save money.

budget_items.what_was_said: Presenter said Lunenburg's five-year change was low compared with comparison towns.

A member estimated a multi-million gap in total spending and guessed Chapter 70 as a possible source.
Presenter said Lunenburg's schedule is the lowest in the comparison range, hurting hiring and retention.

decisions.decision: Chair agreed to take the guest advisers first, out of agenda order.
Advisers will send their white paper on prudent investing to town officials and the task force.
A member will share contact names for two forensic accounting firms with whoever wants them.
The adviser will send the statute sections defining excludable debt and the related legislation.
A town official will reach out and dig through history on the dropped miscellaneous non-recurring category.
The task force will next hear from stakeholders (town employees, department heads, unions), and capital planning is on a separate meeting; members will also draft questions for comparison towns.

what_happened.line: The task force took no votes; its only motion was to adjourn.
Two investment advisers explained a new prudent-investor law that would let trust funds be invested beyond the legal list, with town meeting approval; stabilization and CPA funds are excluded.
Members asked about earning more on cash held in bank and liquid accounts, and an adviser agreed some could be moved to laddered treasuries.
Members presented state (DLS) spending comparisons with other towns, covering health insurance, debt service, recycling, busing, special education and teacher pay.
Follow-ups were assigned, including statute sections on excludable debt, research on a dropped spending category, and stakeholder input from employees, department heads and unions.

why_it_matters: Investing trust-fund money more broadly would need a town meeting vote, so residents may be asked to approve a change in how the town's affordable housing and similar trust funds are invested.
The comparison work on health insurance, debt service and school costs bears on how large the gap between spending and the levy cap looks, and so on what the next budget asks of taxpayers.
